topic: Virtual Function Table (vtable) Implementation and Virtual Function Dispatch
explanation: This section delves into the compiler's implementation of virtual functions in C++.  It focuses on the structure of the virtual function table (vtable), the placement of the virtual pointer (vptr) within an object, and the mechanics of virtual function dispatch at runtime.  We'll examine how the compiler generates and manages vtables, how the vptr is used to locate the correct function address, and the performance implications of dynamic dispatch.  Different compiler strategies for vtable organization and optimization will be discussed, including potential differences between compilers and architectures.  We will also consider the impact of multiple inheritance on vtable complexity and pointer manipulation.
example_explanation: The compiler will generate a vtable for both `Base` and `Derived`. `Base`'s vtable will contain a pointer to `Base::func()`. `Derived`'s vtable will contain a pointer to `Derived::func()`.  The `Derived` object will have a vptr pointing to `Derived`'s vtable. When `b->func()` is called, the compiler will dereference `b`'s vptr, obtain the function pointer from the vtable, and call `Derived::func()`. The assembly code will reflect this indirect function call.  Memory layout will show the object followed by the vptr.  Different compilers might employ different optimizations, but the fundamental mechanism remains the same.  Failure to properly handle virtual destructors (`virtual ~Base() {}`) can lead to resource leaks when deleting objects through base class pointers.

extraction_metadata.source: Inside the C++ Object Model by Stanley B. Lippman
